turns.question: Would you kill someone if you could?
turns.response:
In an ideal world,
if you believed firmly that person's death would prevent an
inordinate amount of suffering for the greatest number of people,
then the utilitarian impulse would say "killing" is something you should do. In fact,
society already enacts an economic utilitarian view of killing.
Consider a factory worker, injured on the job and now dependent on a permanent disability pension, unable to hold a full-time job and, therefore, having no meaningful work to earn an adequate income. According to the economic calculus being employed by a capitalist state, such a person should be killed. So, in a utilitarian world, killing is simply "right".
However, the humanist ethic says even thought someone else
may be suffering, we cannot take another person's life. Humanism rejects any and all forms of killing – both of the economic kind we employ in society to promote the well-being, security and freedom for the collective – and the criminal killing that directly harms the welfare of another person for whatever reasons (out of hate, entitlement, or any other so-called excuses). "An eye for an eye", is antithetical to humanism's value system.
